## Findings by module

### 8

- **refined** (ch-004 (Prologue)): Reader frames the book as a 'biography' of Africa by process, not period (ecology, geology, biology). His central puzzle: modern humans left Africa about 100,000 years ago, and by AD 1500 the out-of-Africa population is estimated at just over 300 million while Africa's grew from about 1 million to 47 million, 'in stable biological equilibrium' (population estimates he cites: 20 million by AD 200, 47 million by AD 1500). He explains the gap by Africa's ecology (soils, disease) rather than by the slave trade, which gives a third position next to Rodney (slave trade arrested population) and Manning; and the figures are estimates with unnamed sources (his notes). Use in Module 8 numbers lesson as another 'who counted it' case; do not quote as fact. He also says 'civilisation' was first outside Africa for metallurgy, agriculture, writing and cities, which the course contradicts for Egypt and Nubia (African), and Jenne-jeno's cities.
- **refined** (ch-039 (population 47 million in 1500)): Reader cites a demographic back-projection of about 47 million for sub-Saharan Africa in 1500; it is an estimate extrapolated from 1900-35, not a count, and the argument that few large cities existed leans on 1945 figures. Label [THIN EVIDENCE]; Rodney and Manning/Nunn give other numbers.
- **refined** (ch-040 chunk 1 (trade totals: Curtin, Lovejoy)): Reader: Curtin 9,391,100 landed 1451-1870; Lovejoy 11,863,000 shipped and 9.6-10.8 million landed; Reader says up to 13 million may prove right. Course uses Voyages 12.5 million embarked 1501-1866. Show the older estimates beside Voyages as an estimate range with the date of each, not as a conflict. Reader also gives Lovejoy yearly averages: 2,500 (1450-1600), 18,680 (1601-1700), 61,330 (1701-1800).
- **refined** (ch-041 chunk 1 (African slave traders, moral framing)): Reader says Africans sold brothers and neighbours for self-aggrandisement and compares them to asset-strippers. This is Reader's judgement, and Rodney and Manning/Nunn disagree on how far the trade rested on African choice versus coercion by arms imports. Present as one position in the Module 8 debate.
- **refined** (ch-043 chunk 1 (Brookes figures; abolition dates; 19th-century trade)): Reader gives the Brookes at 454 rated, 600 (earlier chapter), 609 and a poster of 450 within the same book, so quote one with its source or use a range. Reader: 3 million shipped in the 19th century (28 per cent of the total); Royal Navy captured 1,635 ships and freed 160,000; abolition dates Denmark 1803, Britain 1807, US 1808, Netherlands 1814, France 1818. Check against Module 8 abolition lines.
- **contradicted** (ch-028 (Chapter 24, disease and population)): Reader's thesis: Africa's population stayed small (an estimated 47 million by AD 1500, '20 million by AD 200 of which over half in North Africa and the Nile', 'stable biological equilibrium') because tropical disease and tsetse (trypanosomiasis on about two thirds of potentially productive land, bilharzia, hookworm, falciparum malaria) limited population growth and cities, so that the 'answer' to the growth gap is 'because they moved out of Africa'. This is an environmental-determinist rival to Rodney's slave-trade explanation of stagnation (Module 8) and to Diop's abundance thesis. The numbers are estimates cited without source names in the text (his notes 2 and 3); the claim that disease 'sap[ped] the energy' of Egyptian farmers so that pharaonic power rested on their illness is speculation. Present as a third position and tag [CONTESTED]; do not combine with Rodney's.
- **contradicted** (ch-032 (Chapter 28, slavery inside Africa)): Reader argues against a 'Merrie Africa' view: slavery and 'rights in persons' were commonplace in precolonial Africa, citing a history of slavery claiming 30 to 60 per cent of the population were slaves 'during historical times' (notes 3-4, unnamed in the text), pawning, bridewealth as transactions in persons, Igbo raiding before the 18th century, Tuareg slave integration, traders on the Sahara-Sahel margin owning over 1,000 slaves by the 11th century, and the Atlantic trade as an extension of an internal market. This contradicts Rodney's claim that 'in Africa there were few slaves and certainly no epoch of slavery' (Chapter 2) and Diop's benign picture of slave status, and fits Module 8 lesson 2 ('other slave trades') and Module 3 (Almoravid/Ahmad Baba). The 30 to 60 per cent figure is a contested estimate from one study; tag [CONTESTED] and show all three positions. Reader's 'extension of the internal market' sentence is an interpretation that other historians (Thornton, Manning) argue differently.
- **extended** (ch-035 chunk 2 (Azurara, Lagos 1444)): Reader: Portuguese raids from 1441, first licensed slave voyage 1444 (six caravels, 230 captives); Azurara counts 927 captives 1441-46. Eyewitness basis for the start of the Atlantic trade in Module 8.
- **extended** (ch-036 chunk 1 (Arguim, horses-for-slaves, El Mina)): Reader: horses traded for ten to fifteen slaves (Cadamosto); Jolof elites raided to buy mounts; El Mina founded 1482, gold about half a tonne a year by early 1500s; Akan bought slaves with gold; Portuguese acted as middlemen in existing African exchange. Supports the Module 8 point that African rulers were active partners and that the Portuguese outflanked trans-Saharan gold.
- **extended** (ch-038 (Portuguese conquest of Swahili towns 1503-05)): Reader: Zanzibar 1503, Mombasa and Kilwa 1505 fell to cannon-armed ships; town rivalry blocked joint defence. Context for Module 6 ending.
- **extended** (ch-040 chunk 1 (shares by destination)): Reader (Curtin): under 5 per cent landed in what is now the USA, 42 per cent Caribbean, 38 per cent Brazil; 10-20 per cent died at sea. Good quick check for Module 8. Also: Caulker family of Shenge were slavers; present-day descendants openly acknowledge it, a useful example of African participation.
- **extended** (ch-040 chunk 1 (Hawkins voyages 1562-65; Spanish asientos)): Reader: Hawkins took 300 captives by force or piracy in 1562, about 400 in 1564-65, and met serious African resistance at a Sierra Leone town; Spain issued licences from 1518 for 4,000 captives to the Caribbean. Possible short case for Module 8 on European interlopers breaking the Portuguese monopoly.
- **extended** (ch-040 chunk 2 (Middle Passage records)): Reader: Newton's first voyage lost 16 per cent of 174 captives and 23 per cent of crew; Brookes plan capacity 454, carried 600 in 1783; 1788 act capped numbers by tonnage with bonuses for under 3 per cent mortality. Primary-source-based detail for the Middle Passage lesson; the Brookes figures are as Reader reports them, check against a second source before quoting.
- **extended** (ch-041 chunk 1 (cowries and manillas)): Reader: cowries from the Maldives reached West Africa from about 1515; 6,370 cowries per adult at Forcados 1520; West Africa imported about 11,000 tonnes in the 1700s; manillas at El Mina 287,813 in 1504-07; Richard Miles recorded 2,352 purchases 1772-80 with African buyers dictating the goods. Shows African traders as price-setting partners. Cowrie tonnage conversions are Reader's own arithmetic.
- **extended** (ch-041 chunk 2 (Miles barter lists; Antera Duke diary)): Reader: Richard Miles bought 2,352 captives from 295 dealers, only 11 regular, so many sellers were small traders, not just state elites; Antera Duke's 1785-88 diary (Old Calabar, Efik) is a rare African-authored source, original destroyed in WWII, transcription published 1956. Good primary-source case for Module 8 (African agency). Reader's claim that Efik derives from a root meaning oppress is not verified; leave out.
- **extended** (ch-042 chunk 1 (transformation debate: Lovejoy vs Eltis)): Reader sets out Lovejoy and Manning (trade transformed African societies, slavery expanded in the 19th century) against Eltis (little effect on Africa's course; changes came from inside). Reader says the evidence does not settle it and then sides with transformation. Add Lovejoy and Eltis as named positions in Module 8, tag [CONTESTED]; note Reader's own lean.
- **extended** (ch-042 chunk 1 (Manning model: 21 million captured, population flat 1750-1850)): Reader reports Manning: 9 million shipped 1700-1850 implied about 21 million captured (7 million kept in Africa, 12 million died within a year), and sub-Saharan population roughly flat 1750-1850. Model-based [PROBABLE or CONTESTED]; check wording against the existing Manning/Nunn line in Module 8 before use.
- **extended** (ch-042 chunk 1 (Equiano; Dogon refuge; enslavement by judicial sentence)): Reader: Equiano taken aged 11, Igbo; Freetown 1850 held over 200 languages; one-third taken in war, one-third kidnapped, one-third sold by kin or after conviction; Moore (1730s) says punishments turned into sale; Miller's slaving frontier; Dogon cliff settlement linked to slave raids (a Reader inference). Module 5 non-state societies (Igbo) and Module 8.
- **extended** (ch-042 chunk 1 (maize and cassava)): Reader: maize and cassava reached Africa in the 16th century but became significant for diet only by about the 18th; cassava stores underground up to two years. Check Module 8's Columbian exchange wording against this; labelled as Reader's timing.
- **extended** (ch-042 chunk 2 (guns and iron)): Reader: British exports of 283,000-394,000 guns a year to West Africa 1750-1807 and a 20 million total estimate (Inikori-type figures; Reader cites as best estimates); Luanda 1759 check found only 200 of 4,000 guns serviceable; Dutch director 1705 said the Gold Coast had become a Slave Coast; imported iron displaced African smelting but not smithing (Reader's claim, in tension with Module 1 iron lesson and Rodney; label as contested).
- **extended** (ch-043 chunk 2 (slavery inside Africa grew after abolition)): Reader: after 1807 domestic slavery grew (Asante, Ibadan 104 families with over 50,000 slaves, Sahel 30-50 per cent enslaved by 1900, Sokoto caliphate about 2.5 million in 1900, Zanzibar over 100,000 from the 1830s, Kenyan coast 44 per cent in 1875-84, Nile valley 4 per cent in 1820 to a third by 1900); 1,650,000 sold across the Sahara and Red Sea in the 19th century. Follows Lovejoy; Reader's population shares come from colonial French and other officials' counts, label [PROBABLE]. Supports the existing Module 8 Lovejoy line and Module 4 Sokoto.
- **extended** (ch-043 chunk 2 (Sierra Leone, Liberia)): Reader: Nova Scotia settlers 1792 to Freetown; American Colonization Society 1816-17, Liberia 1821 land taken at gunpoint for under 300 dollars of goods. Post-1807 context; keep to one line in Module 8 as aftermath, not core.
- **extended** (ch-044 chunk 1 (legitimate trade; slave replenishment; drought)): Reader: legitimate trade (palm oil, groundnuts) leaned on slave labour; Senegal groundnuts 27,000 tonnes a year 1868-77 from 70,000 small farmers; Zanzibar needed up to 20,000 imports a year; Reader's estimate 600,000 enslaved inside Africa a year in the 19th century is an assumption chain, [THIN EVIDENCE]; Kongo capital fell from 5,000 to 100 people in 1774-1790s; slave exports peaked in the 1784-95 drought. Climate-and-slavery link is Reader's and Miller's argument, label as such.
- **extended** (ch-051 chunk 1 (Berlin Conference 1884-5)): Reader: no African was invited or consulted at Berlin; treaties were drafted in European languages with untranslatable land terms; Lewanika of the Lozi sought British protection. Supports the Module 8 Berlin lesson; Berlin did not itself carve up the map (that came from later bilateral agreements), so keep the wording to what the book says and check the course line.
- **extended** (ch-052 chunk 1 (colonial boundaries; 177 culture areas)): Reader: borders divide at least 177 ethnic culture areas; Berlin demanded effective occupation; Bismarck reversed on colonies in 1884; Africa about 5 per cent of Britain's trade in the 1870s. Post-1885 context, one line for Module 8. Reader dates Bismarck's fall to 1899-1900 (a slip; he left office in 1890), so do not quote those dates from this book.
- **note** (ch-038 (violence and archaeology)): Reader suggests lack of archaeological evidence for conflict before European contact (except Jebel Sahaba), and warns that the evidence switch from archaeology to documents distorts the picture. Useful caution for Module 1 and 8; speculative, label as one author's inference.

### 1

- **confirmed** (ch-022 and ch-023 (Chapters 18-19, pastoralism and Bantu)): Reader confirms the course's Bantu material: Bantu is a purely linguistic label coined by Bleek with no ethnic meaning; Guthrie's word-root analysis puts the cradle in the Benue valley and Cameroon grassfields; dispersal began about 5,000 years ago; expansion slow in forest (22 km per decade), faster beyond; farmers in the lakes region by about 2,500 years ago and the southern limit by the 4th century AD; 'more than 600' languages (some authorities 300). Course Module 1 lesson 3 says 500+ languages and 4,000 to 5,000 years: consistent, but the language count varies by author and should be given as a range. Also confirms 'Bantu is a language family, not a tribe', and Greenberg's rejection of the Hamitic stereotype (Seligman 1930).
- **confirmed** (ch-027 (Chapter 23, Jenne-jeno)): Reader's detailed account of Jenne-jeno confirms Module 1 lesson 4 (urbanism without kings, before regular trans-Saharan trade) and supplies figures the course lacks or gives differently: about 1,600 years of continuous occupation, a 33 hectare mound with 25 satellite mounds (69 hectares in all), up to about 27,000 people around AD 800, a mud-brick wall 3.6 m thick at the base with no sign of a ruling elite, craft specialisation from the earliest levels (iron, pottery, beads, net weights, spindle whorls), trade mostly in delta food, and a fall to one tenth in the 12th to 14th centuries. Course says occupation from about 250 BCE and tags population figures 'debated': keep the tag, present 27,000 as the McIntosh estimate Reader reports, and use the wall's puzzle (flood or market control) as an example of an unresolved interpretation. Also confirms 'cities without citadels' and heterarchy ideas without the word.
- **contradicted** (ch-023 (Chapter 19, origin of iron-working)): Reader argues iron-smelting in sub-Saharan Africa was 'almost certainly an imported skill' via Phoenician and Berber traders, because no copper-smelting precedent exists (the Agadez claim was dismissed in 1988), citing Taruga on the Jos plateau as the earliest furnaces (about 2,600 years ago) and a camel arrival in the Sahara in the 2nd century AD. Course Module 1 lesson 3 tags the independence of West African iron as [CONTESTED] and notes the radiocarbon plateau. Show Reader's diffusion argument as one side (1998), and note that Diop (both books) and Rodney give the Kush/independent-origin side; newer work (outside these books, not verified) reopened the question. Do not state either as fact. Reader's claim that iron-smelting stands as an 'economic revolution' with no weapons found is also a generalisation; Reader on deforestation by charcoal (one tonne charcoal for three hoes in a Malawi experiment) is a good worked number.
- **contradicted** (ch-024 (Chapter 20, Nile as a corridor)): Reader rejects the idea of the Nile as a corridor that carried civilisation south ('the Nile was a cul-de-sac'), says no Meroitic material has been found west of the Nile, and that iron-smelting is older in West and Central Africa than at Meroe so cannot have come from it. This contradicts Rodney's and Diop's use of Kush as a source of iron, brass and state ideas. It also sits oddly with Reader's own ch. 19 claim that iron was imported from Carthage by Berbers; his two chapters conflict on the origin of West African iron. Present all three positions in Module 1 lesson 3 and tag [CONTESTED].
- **contradicted** (ch-038 (state formation is recent and externally driven)): Reader argues that every sub-Saharan state, from Mali to Zimbabwe, has origins entangled with foreign trade, and that the archaeology shows little coercive centralisation before it. This is one author's thesis and sits against the course's Kush, Aksum, Jenne-jeno and Nok material (Jenne-jeno being a non-state urban cluster supports him in part). Show as a debated position, not a fact.
- **extended** (ch-021 (Chapter 17, cattle, sorghum, pottery, Nabta Playa)): Reader reviews the cattle-domestication dispute (indigenous in the Nile valley, or introduced from the Near East; mtDNA evidence favours a single domestication shared by Europe and Africa, so introduction is 'the greater probability'; goats and sheep certainly introduced), Nabta Playa's village (9,500 to 7,000 years ago; wells, granaries, possibly cultivated sorghum from about 8,000 years ago), pottery in the central Sahara by about 9,500 years ago, and an abrupt aridification about 7,000 years ago pushing herders to the Nile, where Pharaonic agriculture combined these with Near Eastern barley and emmer. A model of how the course's Module 1 evidence tags work (archaeology plus linguistics plus genetics, each with a blind spot): the Nilo-Saharan root words for cow predicted by linguistics (10,000 years) are 'requires archaeological confirmation'. Strong teaching example of two kinds of evidence disagreeing. Dates are Reader's secondary sources.
- **note** (ch-005 (Part One, Chapter 1 'Building a Continent')): Geology: Africa's cratons (West African, Congo, Kaapvaal), the Barberton greenstones, the Witwatersrand gold and the Bushveld Igneous Complex, and the claim that South African minerals financed apartheid. Background for Module 7/8 on mineral wealth and the ecology of the continent; no claim here conflicts with or supports a lesson. Used at most as a one-line ecological backdrop.
- **note** (ch-006 to ch-008 (Chapters 2 to 4, deep time, primates, climate)): Deep-time Africa: earliest life, dinosaurs and Megazostrodon, continental drift, primate evolution at the Fayum, orbital climate cycles and aridity. No lesson in the pre-colonial course depends on it. Relevant only as background for Module 1's remark that the Sahara was green and dried (orbital precession, which Olivier's glossary also mentions, citing Reader p. 37). Reader's point that competition rather than climate drives speciation is outside scope.
- **note** (ch-027 (Chapter 23, ethnic specialisation in the delta)): Reader argues the delta's myths are 'ecological abstractions' that defined ethnic groups (Marka rice, Bambara millet, Fulani and Tuareg herds, Bozo and Somono fishers) by obligations to each other, which kept peace. A nice case for the Module 5 myth checklist: a myth can encode a rule of land use rather than a historical event. Reader's suggestion that the Black Death hit Jenne-jeno via the Sahara is speculation (his word 'could'); do not teach.

### 2

- **confirmed** (ch-025 (Chapter 21, the Periplus)): Reader confirms and extends the course's Periplus mention (Module 2 lesson 3: Adulis in the Periplus, 1st century CE): the handbook dates to AD 40 to 70, devotes about 450 of 7,000 words (6 per cent) to the coast beyond the Horn, names Rhapta (not located archaeologically), and records Roman Egyptian trade with India and Arabia far larger than with East Africa; no Roman coin has been found in East Africa; the East African coast was under Arabian merchants. Useful corrective for Module 6 lesson 1 (Swahili origins): the first-century coast trade was small and Arabian-led. Pertinent numbers (800 grain sailings a year, 25 per cent Roman import duty) are Reader's secondary figures.
- **contradicted** (ch-024 (Chapter 20, the Nile and Meroe)): Reader says Meroe collapsed in the 2nd century AD, hastened by deforestation from iron smelting and changing Red Sea trade, that Kush conquered Egypt in 730 BC and ruled over sixty years, and that Meroe's gods and pyramids were Egyptian in style (Meroitic 'undeciphered'). Course Module 2 gives Piye c.744-714 BCE, the 25th Dynasty c.744-656 BCE (about 88 years), Meroe's collapse in the 4th century CE, Meroitic readable but not translated, and Kush with 'its own script, gods, queens'. Reader's dates are 'about'; trust the course's tagged ranges, and show Reader's environmental explanation (slag mounds, charcoal) as one more factor beside trade shifts and Aksum, tag [CONTESTED]. The undeciphered claim is loose (script read since Griffith 1911). Reader's 'Kush was an expression of Egyptian civilisation' conflicts with the course warning not to write 'Kush was a copy of Egypt'.
- **contradicted** (ch-026 chunk 2 (Chapter 22, stelae and decline)): Reader gives the standing Aksum stele as one block 21 m high (ten storeys), the 24 m stele taken to Rome in 1937, and the 33 m, over 700 tonne stele fallen and broken in five pieces, with over 140 stelae in the city. Course Module 2 lesson 3 says 'the tallest still standing is about 24 m'; Reader's figures indicate the 24 m stele was the one taken to Rome, so the standing one is about 21 m. Correct the lesson sentence to about 21 m standing, and mention that the 24 m stele was the one returned in 2005 (the course already says returned in 2005). This is a numeric correction to apply in the lesson.
- **extended** (ch-020 (Chapter 16, beginnings of agriculture)): Reader (1998, popular) argues the earliest organised food production comes from the Nile valley and Sahara, not the Near East: Wadi Kubbaniya about 19,000 years ago (nut-grass tubers, catfish), a 'wild Nile' flood about 12,000 to 11,500 years ago, repopulation of the Sahara from about 8,500 years ago with cattle, goats and sheep; Egypt's wheat and barley came later from the Near East. Useful background for Module 2 (Kerma and Nile states) and Module 1 (green Sahara). It corrects both Diop's '10,000-year' Egyptian civilisation (the food-producing system is real and old, the state is c. 3100 BCE) and the Hamitic idea that agriculture came to Africa from outside. The Klasies River 'agriculture' at 70,000 years is a single-site interpretation of burnt geophyte residues, [THIN EVIDENCE] in my judgement, not teachable as agriculture.
- **extended** (ch-026 chunk 1 (Chapter 22, Aksum's rise)): Reader's account: Adulis moved inland as water demand grew (4th-6th century town 4 km from shore), Aksum's highland base (rain, altitude, no tsetse), Sabaean-style inscriptions from the 7th century BCE developing into Ge'ez, monumental temples at Yeha and Haoulti, plough agriculture, teff as an indigenous crop (more than 2.5 million seeds per kg), Aksum as 'sub-Saharan Africa's first indigenous state' with its own coinage (gold, silver and copper) and a 33 m, over 700 tonne monolith. Directly counters Diop (Aksum 'more a word than a reality') and Rodney (Aksum founded by a Sabaean dynasty): Reader shows Sabaean influence grafted onto an indigenous rootstock, with archaeology (Yeha, Adulis, coins, stelae). Add to Module 2 lesson 3 as a three-way comparison. The course's tallest-standing figure (about 24 m) and Reader's 33 m (fallen stele) refer to different monuments; Reader dates the king's conversion to the third century, the course 330s or 340s [PROBABLE]: show the range and prefer Ezana's inscriptions.
- **extended** (ch-026 chunk 2 (Chapter 22, Aksum's decline and the Solomonic legend)): Reader explains Aksum's rise and fall by climate and environment: rainy season extended in the first to fourth centuries, double harvests, then deforestation for charcoal, erosion, loss of Red Sea trade (war in the eastern Mediterranean, Persian control of South Arabia, Adulis destroyed by Arab forces in the early 8th century), end of gold coinage, a rainfall decline from about AD 750 and the elite moving to central Ethiopia by about AD 800; Aksum city about 75 hectares and about 20,000 people by AD 500. He states plainly that the Solomon-Sheba-Menelik legend has no historical basis, the Queen of Sheba is a mythical figure, and the city of Aksum was founded centuries after Menelik. Strongly confirms the course's treatment of the Kebra Nagast as tradition not history (Module 2 lesson 4), and adds the environmental explanation of decline to the course's Aksum material. Populations and areas are archaeological estimates.
- **extended** (ch-037 chunk 1 (Ethiopian envoys 1306, Rombulo 1407)): Reader: thirty Ethiopian envoys reached Avignon, Rome and Genoa in 1306 (recorded by Giovanni da Carignano); Pietro Rombulo reached Ethiopia 1407; Henry IV letter 1400; Covilha stayed in Ethiopia about 30 years. Adds Ethiopia's outward diplomacy to Module 2 and counters the passive-Africa picture; Reader says Aksum collapsed in the 9th century, which the course should treat as [PROBABLE] decline, not a single event.
- **extended** (ch-038 (Alvares, Ethiopia 1520-26)): Reader: Alvares travelled six years in Ethiopia; recorded farming, locust famines, leprosy, no town over 1,600 households, and a request from the king for European craftsmen. Eyewitness source for Module 2 late Ethiopia; Reader also calls Ethiopia Africa's oldest continuous state.

### 5

- **confirmed** (ch-031 (Chapter 27, Igbo-Ukwu and the Igbo)): Reader dates the Igbo-Ukwu burial and its lost-wax bronzes to the 10th century, anchored by mining debris from the source of the metals dated AD 895-1000, rejecting an earlier suggestion of the 13th-15th centuries; the burial held a crown, regalia and 165,000 glass and carnelian beads, an outpost of long-distance trade, in a region otherwise without states (Igbo age-grades, oracles, secret societies). Matches Module 5 lesson 1 (Igbo-Ukwu) and the non-state societies lesson; also supports the course's rule that the Igbo example is an anomaly to explain, not a state. Rodney says the Ibo have made brass and bronze since the 9th century, consistent.
- **refined** (ch-039 (kingship as European label)): Reader argues many African polities called monarchies were cycles of renewal not stages toward states, citing Luganda mirembe and rare primogeniture, versus Roland Oliver who sees monarchy as ancient. Two positions for Module 5 on Oyo, Asante, Dahomey.
- **extended** (ch-029 (Chapter 25, farming, land tenure and elephants)): Reader says African farming was savanna-based and had no single centre; farmers hoed by hand because ploughs and draught animals did not pay in energy terms (tsetse, no forage crops); intensification (terracing, irrigation, manuring) is old and indigenous, with Ukara island (Lake Victoria, over 200 people per km2, stall-fed cattle, privately owned trees and land, no chiefs) as the example; and that 'traditional land tenure throughout Africa granted only rights of use', which supports Diop's no-feudalism claim in Precolonial Black Africa and Rodney's points on land abundance, while Ukara shows private land tenure existed. Add as nuance to Module 5 and the comparison of states: land tenure varied (use-rights nearly everywhere, private ownership on Ukara); the Ukara figures are 20th-century survey data and oral history, and Reader says scholars think dense settlement there dates only from the 17th century. The elephant-as-farming-constraint thesis (competitive exclusion) is a single study; ivory trade claims in Module 6 unaffected.
- **extended** (ch-030 (Chapter 26, age-grades and chiefs)): Reader's model of precolonial political order: precedence ('being first') gives authority; chiefs had status but little power; the age-grade system spread power horizontally and produced gerontocracy; states arose when long-distance trade let some people accumulate wealth and coerce porters and slaves. This is a general explanation, [CONTESTED], that fits the course's non-state societies lesson and contrasts with Diop's 'monarchic Africa everywhere'. Also notes Maasai moran, Dogon initiation cave and Kikuyu fighting; the claim that sub-Saharan Africa had 'no traditions of devastating warfare before the nineteenth century' (Thompson) conflicts with the course's account of Mapungubwe/Great Zimbabwe's fortified hilltops and Kanem-Bornu raiding, so do not repeat it.
- **extended** (ch-032 (Chapter 28, Benin sacrifices)): Reader reports the remains of forty-one young women, dressed and adorned, at the bottom of a well in Benin City dated before AD 1200 as probably ritual sacrifice by a centralised authority, and says sacrificial pits continued until 1897. Course Module 5 lesson 2 (Benin) mentions earthworks and the 1897 expedition; the pre-1200 date for a Benin sacrifice well is a single archaeological report I cannot verify; use only with 'reported' and no dates.
- **extended** (ch-043 chunk 1 (Oyo, Efik Egbo, Dahomey, Asante)): Reader: Oyo fell through overextension, chiefs' rivalry and a Muslim revolt; Efik of Old Calabar governed through the Egbo society, with Duke Ephraim the last big trader; Dahomey was a small centralised slaving kingdom with primogeniture and ten kings 1650-1889, Agaja's 1726 letter, 10-12,000 exported a year (Dalzell 1763); Asante power built on gold, Osei Tutu, 1701 victory, Kumasi roads, Asantemanhyiamu, trading empire about 250,000 km2 by 1820. Cross-check each date and figure against Module 5 before adding; sacrifice figures (Burton, Bowdich) are visitor reports, label [THIN EVIDENCE].

### 3

- **confirmed** (ch-030 (Chapter 26, salt, camels and the Niger)): Reader confirms and adds depth to Module 3 lesson 3 (trans-Saharan network): camels reached the Sahara via the Horn from southern Arabia, with Berber ancestors of the Tuareg using them for trade between the 2nd and 5th centuries AD (course: regular use in the first centuries CE [PROBABLE]); salt was the first and most important long-distance good (Bilma 70,000 camel-loads a year in Nachtigal's day; Taoudeni and Teghaza slabs of about 30 kg, with debt-bonded miners, still in the 1990s); Timbuktu a clearing-house, with salt markup of sixty times at Gonja and kola at forty times near the salt sources; the 6,400-year-old Dufuna canoe. Reader says nothing about a 1:1 gold-for-salt exchange rate, so Olivier's 'an ounce of gold for an ounce of salt' stays unsupported (our check against this book only). Reader dates horses south of the Sahara in Arabic texts from al-Muhallabi, about AD 985.
- **confirmed** (ch-031 (Chapter 27, Almoravids and Ghana)): Reader cites the review by Conrad and Fisher: 'we have discovered no sources, whether external or internal, which unambiguously point to' an Almoravid conquest of Ghana, the vagueness decreasing as later writers report it. This supports the course's [CONTESTED] tag in Module 3 lesson 2 and contradicts Diop (Precolonial Black Africa), who narrates a conquest of 1076 to 1087 as fact. Reader's own explanation (herds too big, ecology rather than conquest) is a hypothesis, tag [CONTESTED]. Strong two-book comparison for the lesson.
- **extended** (ch-031 (Chapter 27, origin of the trans-Saharan gold trade)): Reader argues gold exports across the Sahara began only after the camel and better climate, around the end of the 3rd century AD: no classical author mentions it, Herodotus does not, Lucan (c. AD 60) says no gold was mined in Africa, Carthaginian gold coins appear 296-311 and rise in the 4th century, solidi until 695, then Arab dinars at Kairouan; West Africa the main gold source from the 11th to 17th centuries (almost two thirds of world output in the later Middle Ages, per his source), gold exchange for copper at two thirds its weight in the early 14th century, and a 12th-century caravan with over 2,000 copper bars. Adds a dating basis for Module 3's 'camels and gold' line. Also: he says gold had no value in indigenous African culture, which is too sweeping (Akan goldwork, Mapungubwe gold) and should not be repeated.

### 4

- **refined** (ch-031 (Chapter 27, Ghana and Koumbi Saleh)): Reader says the figure of 200,000 men with 40,000 archers (al-Bakri) is 'probably a tenfold, or even a twentyfold exaggeration'; Koumbi Saleh is a Muslim traders' town of about 250 hectares with stone houses, a mosque, glass weights for gold and Mediterranean pottery, occupied from the 6th to the 18th century with 15,000 to 20,000 people at its densest; the king's town has not been found, and the 'king' may have been the richest local man. Course Module 4 lesson 1 already notes Kumbi Saleh and Tegdaoust as urban trading centres and that al-Bakri never visited; use these numbers as the archaeological check on al-Bakri's, and note that Diop (Precolonial) took the 200,000 literally. The nugget tethering a horse also appears in Olivier ch. 3: both books repeat the same chroniclers' image.
- **extended** (ch-035 chunk 1 (Leo Africanus, Timbuktu salt)): Reader quotes Leo Africanus on Timbuktu salt prices; usable as a European-era witness in Module 4, labelled as a secondary report.

### 6

- **confirmed** (ch-033 chunk 1 (Chapter 29, bananas, cattle, Ntusi and Bigo)): Reader dates Ntusi to the 11th to 14th or 15th century (hundreds to thousands of people, cattle bones, a smelting industry) and Bigo's ditches (more than ten kilometres, up to five metres into bedrock, 300 hectares enclosed) to the 13th to 16th centuries, as a defended cattle refuge, with cattle-wealth rather than long-distance trade centralising the Great Lakes polities; bananas introduced from South-East Asia by about 2,000 years ago (earliest written record at Adulis in AD 525), linguistic evidence (Schoenbrun) of banana and cattle vocabulary growth AD 500 to 1450. Matches Module 6 lesson 3 (Ntusi and Bigo roughly 11th to 16th centuries [PROBABLE]); Rodney's 'six and a half miles' of ditch (about 10.5 km) agrees with Reader's 'over ten kilometres'. Safe wording: ditches of about ten kilometres. The linguistic dates are reconstruction, tag accordingly.
- **confirmed** (ch-033 chunk 2 (Chapter 29, Hamitic myth in the Great Lakes)): Reader quotes Speke's 'Theory of Conquest of Inferior by Superior Races' (1863) and rejects it: there is no firm evidence of Ethiopian conquerors, no Cushitic substratum is detected, a single Bantu language runs through the region, and Tutsi and Hutu speak the same Bantu language, both descended from farmers 2,000 to 1,500 years ago; he notes the elites themselves perpetuated the myth. Exactly supports Module 6 outcome 'Reject a racial theory of state origins' (Module 6 lesson 3-5) and agrees with Rodney's and Greenberg's rejection. Reader's account of decline of the Bigo-type centres in the 15th-16th centuries and rise of banana-based polities by the 18th supports the course's Buganda lesson (rise of Buganda by 18th century, Rodney says the same). Use Speke's passage as a short paraphrased example of a source that is itself the myth.
- **extended** (ch-035 chunk 1 (Cheng Ho fleets, 1415 giraffe)): Reader mentions Cheng Ho fleets and a giraffe sent to China; supports the Chinese contact line in Module 6, which stays [PROBABLE].
- **extended** (ch-036 chunk 1 (Diogo Cao, Kongo, Nzadi)): Reader: Cao 1483 met the kingdom of Conguo at the river its people called Nzadi (great river); padrao crosses 1482-86. Context for the Kongo lesson.
- **extended** (ch-037 chunk 2 (Swahili towns 1498, Ibn Majid, Malindi)): Reader: Swahili towns (Mocambique, Mombasa, Malindi) were Muslim and wealthy in silk-bordered cottons; Portuguese gifts were scorned; da Gama's pilot was Ahmad ibn Majid. Supports Module 6 Swahili wealth and Indian Ocean pilots; Portuguese Roteiro is a hostile-contact source.
- **extended** (ch-039 (Kongo, Afonso I)): Reader: Mbanza Kongo became a confederation by the mid-1400s; Nzinga Mbemba baptised Afonso 1491, king 1506 to 1543; Kikongo catechism 1555 first printed Bantu text; Afonso's letter says Kongolese were being kidnapped and sold; Portugal replied that Kongo had nothing else to sell. Supports the Module 6 Kongo lesson and Module 8 point that European trade corrupted African polities. Check the course's Afonso date wording.
- **extended** (ch-043 chunk 1 (Kongo decline)): Reader: Kongo had about 5,000 troops incl 500 mercenary musketeers; decline from provincial rebellions and shift of Portuguese trade to Angola in the early 1700s. Compare with Module 6 Kongo decline wording.

### 7

- **confirmed** (ch-047 (Zulu myths and reality: slaving thesis)): Reader's ch-047 backs the course's Module 7 lesson 4: the standard Shaka/Mfecane story is partly a 20th-century construction; Delagoa Bay slave trade (12,000 a year from Mozambique to Brazil and islands by 1812; 1,000-6,000 men a year c.1818-30s; hinterland 100,000-180,000) and Cape frontier labour raids (Dithakong 1823, Mbolompo 1828) are offered as causes, and Reader calls the slaving thesis 'not yet proven'. Contradicts Reader's own ch-044 which puts the cause in drought and Shaka. Use ch-047 as the weightier, better-sourced chapter, and say plainly that the book disagrees with itself.
- **refined** (ch-034 (Chapter 30, Mapungubwe and Great Zimbabwe)): Reader's southern African sequence: Mapungubwe from the 11th century with the hill-top burials by the early 12th, a gold rhinoceros about AD 1200 (earliest indigenous gold use in the south), fading about 1250; Great Zimbabwe built between AD 1275 and 1550 (the Great Enclosure in the 14th century: outer wall 244 m long, 5 m thick, up to 10 m high; Conical Tower 9 m), 11,000 to 18,000 people at its fifteenth-century peak, 78 hectares, a beef-cattle economy (about 80 per cent of cattle slaughtered at 24 to 30 months in elite middens) and a trade link through Renders Ruin finds (Persian bowl, Chinese celadon, a Kilwa coin of the early 14th century, tens of thousands of glass beads); then Torwa (c.1450-c.1650) and Mutapa (c.1450-1700). Course Module 7 gives Great Zimbabwe mostly 12th to 15th centuries by ancestors of the Shona, outer wall up to about 11 m, population 10,000 to 20,000 [CONTESTED], Mutapa from the 15th century. Close agreement; Reader's wall height 10 m versus the course's 11 m, build span 1275-1550 versus 12th-15th: show both and keep the course's tags. Rodney's 'Sotho builders, Rozwi founded Mutapa' is contradicted: Reader says Shona, Torwa and Mutapa as separate successors.
- **refined** (ch-044 chunk 1 (Bantu 'migratory drift'; cattle and maize)): Reader: southern Bantu expansion was a gradual drift not mass conquest; Khoisan and Bantu groups exchanged cattle and roles; cattle-based stratification; maize in Mozambique by 1798 and Zambia (Lacerda) 1798; wet period in the late 1700s. Contradicts any 'sweeping migration' wording in Modules 1 and 7; check and soften. The Mfecane link comes next chapter.
- **refined** (ch-046 chunk 1 (Omer-Cooper's Zulu Aftermath versus archaeology)): Reader sets out Omer-Cooper's classic Mfecane (Shaka as motor; drought and population pressure) and then says Zululand surveys show no general ecological crisis, so the drought-pressure route fails there. This corrects Reader's own ch-044 and gives Module 7 lesson 4 a third column: the older Zulu-centred story, the slaving thesis, and archaeological evidence against local ecological crisis. Zululand farming evidence from AD 600 (villages of several hundred people). Mfengu etymology and Xhosa as 'Ngoni-speakers' not reliable.
- **contradicted** (ch-044 chunk 2 (Mfecane and Shaka)): Reader treats the Mfecane as Zulu expansion driven by drought and population pressure from Shaka's Natal hinterland (1816-40), with Sotho Difaqane naming; Reader also mislabels the Ngoni as the larger group of which the Zulu are a part. Mfecane is itself contested (Cobbing argues it was largely a colonial-era construct and slave-raiding effect); show both with the course Zulu lesson and mark [CONTESTED].
- **extended** (ch-034 (Chapter 30, Great Zimbabwe interpretation)): Reader gives an ecological reading (tsetse-free plateau, beef surplus first, gold control as a corollary), says the building was loosely built drystone (a contractor estimated 84 men could build the complex in two years), that the Zimbabwe birds are 35 cm soapstone, and that environmental damage ended the centre in the late 15th century; and that Shona gold output to the 1890s was at least 200 million grams from over 1,200 reefs. The two-year contractor estimate is a modern illustration and should not be used to claim low effort; the 78 hectare and population figures are estimates. Cattle-and-gold origin story is Reader's thesis; tag [CONTESTED].
- **extended** (ch-037 chunk 1 (da Gama Roteiro 1497-98)): Reader: Roteiro describes Khoisan at St Helena Bay, herders with cattle at Mossel Bay, and a 1498 east-coast stretch with copper, tin, iron-bladed spears and salt-making; at Mocambique Arab dhows with compasses and charts. Eyewitness view of southern and east African societies, a Portuguese source with its own bias.
- **extended** (ch-038 (Sofala gold, 1506)): Reader: the Portuguese were told Sofala could yield 4,000 tonnes of gold a year, yet only 2.6 kg left Sofala in the first fifteen months and exports stayed small to 1513. Corrects any impression that Zimbabwe-era gold flows were huge; the figure is Portuguese hope, not output.
- **extended** (ch-045 (Khoisan pastoralists and the Cape, 1652-1810)): Reader: Khoisan sheep in the Cape from about the 1st century AD, cattle from about the 7th; seasonal migration circuits; about 50,000 Khoisan in the south-western Cape in 1652; the 1659 Khoisan revolt; 1713 smallpox; commandos killed 2,480 Khoisan 1786-95; Zuurveld contact with Xhosa about 1770 and first Frontier War 1779. Reader says Bantu farming reached southern Natal by the 3rd-4th century AD. Adds Khoisan herding and the cattle-sheep chronology to Module 7; keep to pre-1820 and label colonial records as hostile sources. The Xhosa 'branch of Ngoni-speakers' wording is not reliable.
- **extended** (ch-047 (Dithakong, Mantatees, Ordinance 49; Zulu amakhanda)): Reader: the Mantatee 'horde' was a displaced group of about 2,000 (initial claim 30,000-100,000); Dithakong 25-26/06/1823 up to 300 killed; Ordinance 49 of 1828; Zulu amakhanda as relocatable military settlements; Ngwane, Sotho (Moshoeshoe) and proto-Swazi as refuge states. Good worked example of source criticism for Module 7 (missionary reports vs archives). Reader's argument that the Zulu state 'was a product' of Delagoa Bay disturbance is one reading, [CONTESTED].

Totals: 9 confirmed, 10 refined, 8 contradicted, 40 extended, 0 absent, 4 note.
